notes.meaning: Solomon built a massive bronze altar for animal sacrifices in the temple court. It measured thirty feet square and fifteen feet high, which was much larger than the altar Moses made for the tabernacle. Because it was so tall, people standing across the courtyards could see the sacrifices burning. This reminded worshippers of the terrible cost of sin and pointed to God's mercy in forgiving them.

Solomon also made a giant round bronze basin known as the Sea. It was about fifteen feet across, seven and a half feet deep, and forty-five feet around. This enormous pool took the place of the smaller washing basin used in the wilderness tabernacle.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the temple imagery recalled the Garden of Eden, with the Sea picturing either life-giving waters or God subduing the chaotic waters of creation.

notes.meaning: Around the outer wall of the basin ran two rows of carved figures shaped like oxen. These ornamental figures were cast right into the bronze when the basin was poured, making them part of the vessel itself. They added strength and beauty to the rim of the great pool.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars note that the parallel text in 1 Kings describes wild gourds rather than oxen around the rim, which could be an early copyist error since the two Hebrew words look very similar, though others suggest both designs may have been included.

notes.meaning: The great basin rested on the backs of twelve sculpted bronze oxen. Groups of three faced outward toward each of the four main directions of the compass, with their backs turned inward toward the center. Their outward-facing posture gave an impression of strength extending in every direction.

The bronze sides of the basin were about three inches thick, and the upper rim flared outward like an open lily flower. It could hold roughly eighteen thousand gallons of water when completely full. This vast supply ensured there was always plenty of clean water on hand for the priests.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Commentators often harmonize the three thousand baths mentioned here with the two thousand baths in 1 Kings by explaining that three thousand was the total capacity when full to the brim, while two thousand was the amount normally kept inside for daily use.

notes.meaning: Solomon placed ten smaller washbasins in the courtyard, five along the south side and five along the north. The priests used these smaller basins to rinse the meat and parts of the animal offerings before placing them on the altar. The giant Sea was kept separate and used only by the priests to wash their own hands and feet before serving God.

Craftsmen made ten lampstands of solid gold according to the original pattern God gave to Moses. Five were placed along the south wall and five along the north wall inside the temple. Where the tabernacle had only one lampstand, the temple now had ten. This bright increase in light reflected the greater size and glory of God's house.

Ten tables were crafted and placed inside the holy room, five on the south side and five on the north. Solomon also provided one hundred gold bowls used to carry and sprinkle sacrificial blood. These furnishings showed how richly God provided for worship in His house.

Solomon built two courtyards around the temple: an inner court for the priests and a large outer court for the general public. The heavy wooden doors leading into these spaces were covered with bronze plates for strength and beauty. This design kept the sacred space reverent while still welcoming the whole nation to gather and pray.

The great bronze Sea was placed outside at the southeast corner of the temple. It stood between the altar of sacrifice and the entrance to the building. This allowed the priests to wash and purify themselves before stepping into God's presence.

Huram, a master metalworker, cast the ash pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls. With these items, he finished all the bronze work King Solomon hired him to do for the house of God. These everyday tools were essential for keeping the altar clean and orderly during daily worship.

Huram crafted the two giant bronze pillars that stood at the temple entrance, along with their bowl-shaped tops. He covered each top with a woven metal network to form a decorative band. Hanging from these networks were four hundred sculpted pomegranates arranged in two rows on each capital.

Huram also made ten movable bronze stands along with the ten basins that sat on top of them. These wheeled stands allowed the priests to roll water wherever it was needed in the courtyard. Every piece was built to assist in the practical work of preparing the sacrifices.

The list of bronze work also included the single large Sea and the twelve sculpted oxen supporting it. Placing this massive pool on sculpted animals made it one of the most striking objects in the temple courts. It stood as a permanent reminder that worship requires clean hearts and hands.

The craftsman Huram-abi made the cooking pots, ash shovels, meat forks, and all their related tools out of polished bronze. Solomon honored him by calling him 'father,' a title of respect given to great artists and master builders. Every item he cast was buffed to a bright, shiny finish before being placed in the temple.

The king had all these large bronze items cast in the Jordan River valley between Succoth and Zeredah. That region had thick, clay-rich soil that was ideal for shaping foundry molds. Pouring the molten metal there kept the smoky, industrial work away from the sacred temple hill in Jerusalem.

Solomon produced such a huge quantity of bronze articles that no one even tried to weigh them. The amount of metal was simply too great to count or record. This lavish work showed that Solomon spared no expense in honoring the Lord.

Solomon also provided all the golden furnishings for the inside of the temple, including the incense altar and the tables. These tables held the Bread of the Presence, which were twelve loaves placed before God each week as a sacred offering. This holy bread symbolized God's continual fellowship with the twelve tribes of Israel and His faithful care for them.

Craftsmen made the lampstands of pure gold and their oil lamps, which burned in front of the inner sanctuary. The priests kept these lamps trimmed and burning according to the exact instructions God gave through Moses. Their steady glow lit the holy room day and night.

The decorative flower blossoms, the lamps, and the wick tongs were all made of the highest quality gold. Each branch of the lampstands was shaped like a flowering plant to reflect the beauty of life in God's presence. The writer emphasizes that only the purest gold was used for the tools nearest to God.

All the smaller tools—wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, ladles, and incense pans—were made of pure gold, and the temple doors were covered with gold plating. This gold covered the inner doors leading into the Most Holy Place as well as the main entrance to the building. The shimmering gold on every surface pointed to the holiness, beauty, and purity of God's earthly dwelling.
